intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: You wake inside a locked data center. Four sealed rooms stand between you and the exit, each holding one piece of a single paper on distributed computation.

intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: Understand each room's piece, and its door will open.

rooms.title: The Two Function Room
rooms.description: Two consoles glow, one labeled MAP and one labeled REDUCE, each waiting for the right behaviour to be loaded into it.

rooms.title: The Examples Room
rooms.description: Four dusty case files sit on a table, each describing a different task that was once run through this system.

rooms.title: The Pipeline Room
rooms.description: A wall-sized diagram of workers, splits, and disks hangs crooked, its numbered steps scattered and waiting to be reattached.

rooms.title: The Design Room
rooms.description: A blank whiteboard and a half-finished word-count program sit under a flickering lamp, daring you to finish the design.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: apply the Map/Reduce model to a design you haven't seen stated outright, to prove you understand the model rather than one memorized example.

item.scenario: A teammate proposes a map/reduce design for tallying how many times each URL was requested across a huge set of web logs, fitting map (k1,v1) → list(k2,v2) and reduce (k2,list(v2)) → list(v2).
item.prompt: Which design matches how URL access frequency is actually counted?

options.text: Map outputs (URL, 1) for each log entry; Reduce adds together all the values for that URL and emits a total count pair.
options.feedback: This matches the described design: map outputs 〈URL,1〉, and reduce adds the values together into a total count.

options.text: Map tallies the counts directly and emits a finished total; Reduce just copies that total through unchanged.
options.feedback: Counting is reduce's job once values are grouped by key; map should only emit the raw 〈URL,1〉 pairs, not a finished total.

options.text: Map outputs (1, URL) pairs so they can be sorted by count; Reduce groups them alphabetically by URL.
options.feedback: Swapping the key breaks the grouping: values need to be keyed by URL so reduce can merge all counts for the same URL, not sorted by the count itself.

sourceRefs.quote: The map func- tion processes logs of web page requests and outputs 〈URL,1〉.
The reduce function adds together all values for the same URL and emits a 〈URL,total count〉 pair.

hints: Ask which function should only emit raw pairs, and which one does the actual merging of values sharing a key.

outro.speaker: archive
outro.text: The last console hums and the exit seal lifts. You didn't just recall the model — you applied it.

intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: The lights in this wing are timed to old benchmark logs. Three rooms hold what really happened when this system was pushed to its limits.

rooms.title: The Timing Room
rooms.description: Stopwatches on the wall show conflicting numbers for the same grep and sort runs, daring you to tell true readings from false ones.

rooms.title: The Usage Room
rooms.description: A corkboard pinned with Google product names waits to be split into two piles: general techniques and web-data mining.

rooms.title: The Straggler Room
rooms.description: A single worker machine blinks red and slow on a rack of otherwise healthy ones, its fate hanging on how backup tasks actually work.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: rebuild the straggler timeline from the disabled-backup-tasks run, the exact scenario backup tasks exist to prevent.

item.prompt: The exit lock wants the backup-disabled sort run's ending rebuilt in order.

steps.text: After 960 seconds, all except 5 of the reduce tasks are completed.
These last few stragglers don't finish until 300 seconds later.
The entire computation takes 1283 seconds, an increase of 44% in elapsed time.

item.why: This is the exact sequence the paper reports for the sort job once backup tasks were disabled, showing why stragglers at the end cost so much time.

sourceRefs.quote: After 960 seconds, all except 5 of the reduce tasks are completed.
However these last few stragglers don’t fin- ish until 300 seconds later.
The entire computation takes 1283 seconds, an increase of 44% in elapsed time.

hints: Think about what happens between the 960-second mark and the moment the whole job is finally declared done.

outro.speaker: archive
outro.text: The rack's red light goes dark and the final door slides open. You've seen exactly what a straggler costs — and why backups exist.
